drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White's queen on h5 was hoping to win back your f5 pawn, which nothing defends, and to keep your queen busy far from home. Qxa3 grabs a pawn, but it lets White answer Qxf5 and follow with Rc1, so you slid from +7.3 to roughly +5. What you missed is that your queen on d3 already attacks the rook on d1. Even with Re1 guarding it, Qxd1 forces Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1, and you've traded queens and come out a rook for a bishop ahead, with ...e4 kicking the knight next. When you're already crushing, take the biggest thing on the board and simplify instead of collecting pawns.
drills.threat: White's queen on h5 targets your loose f5 pawn, while your own queen on d3 has wandered deep into his camp.

drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White wanted to win your loose bishop on h4, or at least chase it around while he untangled. Bf6 saves the piece, but then Ng5 jumps in, Bxg5 Qxg5 f4 follows, and White has pushed your pieces back. You went from +6.8 to about +5.2. Bxf2+ works better because the bishop can capture with check before it leaves. After Kh1 Bf7 your bishop hits the queen on h5, while the bishop on f2 still eyes the rook on e1, so Qg5 Bxe1 Rxe1 wins you the exchange. Before you retreat an attacked piece, check whether it can take something with check first.

drills.title: vs AlfredoPig (770) — Four Knights Game Double Spanish Variation
drills.coachNote: White wanted to kick your queen off c5 and use the tempo to break in along the c-file and onto the seventh rank, with his queen on a5 already aimed at c7. Qb6 steps away passively, and White replies Nf5, then Rd7, Qc3 and Qg6, so his pieces flood in and you fell from equal to nearly lost, a 3.9-pawn swing. Qe3 is the answer: from e3 your queen hits the rook on c1, the knight on g3, and the d3 and f4 pawns all at once. Even after Qxc7 you have Qxd3+ Ka1 Rd7, which chases his queen off c7, and after Qe5 the game is level. When your queen is attacked, look for the square where she makes threats of her own.

drills.coachNote: White wanted dxc4, opening the d-file so his queen and rook line up against your rook on d8. A quiet a5 ignores that tension, and White answers Ng3, then Qe2, piling onto c4, so you slipped from +1.2 to about -1.2. The move that uses the tension is cxd3, taking first. After Ng3 dxc2+ Qxc2 Rxd1+ Rxd1 your pawn lands on c2 with check, you net a pawn, and the rooks come off. If you have a pawn capture that comes with check, cash it in before your opponent takes the same decision away from you.

drills.title: vs Wuranti (790) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black was threatening to win your bishop on d3, which is hit twice, by the knight on b4 and the bishop on g6, and guarded only by your queen. Qb3 attacks the knight, but Black just plays Bxd3, and after Nxa7 Kxa7 Qxb4 the knights trade off while you've lost a bishop for a pawn. That is a 4.3-pawn swing from a healthy position. The engine's top choice is the sharp Rc7, backed by Nb5, which drags his queen off d7 with Qxc7 Nxc7 before Bxd3 lands. The calmer Bxg6 or Be2 also solve it. Before you attack something of his, count what's attacking your own pieces.

drills.coachNote: Black's bishop on d6 was challenging your Bf4, and his king on c8 has an undefended a7 pawn in front of it, so your knight on c3 had a shot ready. Nb5 hits d6 and a7 at once, and after Bxf4 Nxa7+ Kc7 exf4 you've taken a pawn with check and recaptured on f4. Then Black's ...Bxd3 has to be handled with care. drills.coachNote: White's plan is to squeeze you on the eighth rank: the d6 pawn checks you and attacks the e7 knight, and the rook on b6 is one step from b8. Kd8 walks onto that rank, so Rb8+ arrives with check and forces Nc8 to block. Then c6 and Rh7 pick your position apart. You were already worse at -2.7, but this turned it into a lost game, a 7.9-pawn swing. Kc8 keeps the king off that line, because Rb8+ just runs into Kxb8. After c6 Bc4 dxe7 Kc7 Rb7+ you've lost the knight but you're still in the game. When your king is in check, look at which squares his rook can check from next.

drills.coachNote: White wants to take on c5 with tempo and use the open c-file against your king on c8. Meanwhile his pawn on d5 is completely unprotected, and your knight on e7 attacks it. Kd7 ignored both facts: Rxc5 won the pawn for free, Rc8 pushed you around, and e6+ drove your king back to d8. The position was about equal at -0.1, and that sequence cost you 3.0 pawns. Nxd5 grabs the loose pawn and puts the knight on a strong central square. After Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6 things stay balanced. When something is hanging, take it before you shuffle the king.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White was in a mating net and had only one hope: untangle with Nb1-d2 and get his queen and rook back into the game. You had mate in one, with a huge +20 eval. Rxb2 grabbed a pawn instead, gave him time for Nd2, Qc2 and Rh2, and after Qxd3 his position had come back to life. You still won, but you threw away a forced mate and about 15 pawns of advantage. Qg2# is the move: your queen slides down the c6-g2 diagonal, the rook on f2 protects it, and the king has no escape. Before any quiet capture, check every check.

drills.coachNote: White's plan is Re1 to challenge your bishop on e5, then b3 to free the knight on b1. You were clearly winning here, up nearly five pawns by the engine's count. a6 is a slow queenside move that gave him all the time he needed: Re1, Rde8, b3, and h5 (about 1.7 pawns given back). Qf3 is sharper. It puts your queen deep in his camp, and your rook on f8 lines up with it against f2 and h3. After Rd1 Rde8 Re1 Bd6 your pieces are all active and you keep the initiative. When you're winning, put your pieces on active squares before making quiet pawn moves.

drills.coachNote: Black's only hope is to shuffle his king between e7 and f7 while every pawn is blocked, hoping you can't find a way to make progress. You were completely winning at +19.8, and the engine also accepts Kf4, so this isn't a disaster. The line Kf4 Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 gets to the same setup as Kf3, so you didn't lose much. Kf3 is the cleaner route: after Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 Kf7 your king stands behind the e-pawn and Black is nearly out of moves. Keep the king route and the pawn plan (e4, then Ke3) clear in your head before you step.

drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Black's king is stuck babysitting the e6 pawn, so your plan is to walk your own king round to b5 and start eating queenside pawns. That route runs through c4, where your bishop was standing, and Bb3 clears it. It isn't a losing move, but look at the line: Bb3 Ke7 Kc4 Kf7 Ba2 has you playing Ba2 anyway, so you burned a whole tempo, and tempo is what wins these positions. Ba2 gets the bishop to its final square on the same diagonal, still pressing e6, so Ke7 Kc4 Ke8 Kb5 Kd8 has your king arriving with Black running low on useful moves. When a piece has to clear the road, send it straight to where it will stay.

You were winning at +5.6 and lost the game in one move. Qd7+ is a check, so Black has to move his king (Kf6) and gets no time for Qxd2. drills.coachNote: White's a- and b-pawns on the sixth are the real danger. Once b7 is played, your rook has to stop a queen, and his king on e4 is close enough to help. drills.coachNote: Black's queen on d2 is giving check along the second rank. Your king has to deal with it, and the bishop on f7 covers the diagonal to f3. Kf3 walks straight into that: Bd5+ forces Be4, Bxe4+ drags your king out to f4, and the attack there is decisive. You were winning by about 4.5 pawns and it flipped to roughly -12. Re2 blocks the check instead, and the rook is guarded by your bishop on d3 and your king on f2. Black's queen can only take it by giving itself up for a rook: Qxe2+ Bxe2, and you're a queen for a rook up. You even get to pick up the f7 bishop later with Nxf7. Qxc5 grabs a pawn but drops the queen's grip on the seventh rank. After f4+ gxf4 b6 you're forced back to d5 to keep guarding the knight, and a position that was +19.9 becomes only about +7. Qf7 is the stronger move. It attacks the loose rook on e8 and pins Black's king to the h8 corner. Black's rook has to run to b8, and then Nd7 attacks it again while f4+ gxf4 g5 is all the counterplay Black has left. When you're crushing, go after the king and loose pieces rather than a pawn.

Rd2 puts your rook next to White's king and queen, protected only by that same e3 pawn. So Nxe3 removes the pawn and leaves the rook hanging. You have to trade Rxg2 Nxg2, and White has swapped a queen for a rook and kept a piece. That took you from +12 to about +7. Qh4+ is the better way. The check goes down the h4–e1 diagonal, forcing Nf2, and exf2+ takes it with another check. After Kf1 Rd1+ Ke2 White's king is on the run with all your pieces still there. When you're winning big, use checks that force White's moves before you commit a piece.
